prompt: Some people say the best person to learn from is someone who is excellent at the thing. Others say the best teacher is someone who once found it hard and remembers how they got through. Which makes the better teacher? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response settles early on what it means by better, since teaching that produces fast progress and teaching that keeps a beginner going are not the same standard. Two examples explored closely will do more than five named in passing. The strongest papers grant the expert's advantage honestly before explaining why it does not decide the question.
accessibility_note: A student can answer this from any teacher they have had, including a classmate or an older student, so no access to coaching or private instruction is assumed.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "I had rehearsed the apology all week, and when the moment came I said something else entirely."
guidance: A strong story stays inside the scene the opening line hands it rather than reaching back to explain the whole history first; the reader can learn what happened from what is said now. Look for a narrator whose account of their own behaviour is interesting because it is not entirely reliable. The ending should follow from what was said instead of the apology, not undo it.
accessibility_note: The sentence supplies the situation completely, and needing to apologize for something is not tied to any particular setting or background.

prompt: Do you agree that a person is better judged by how they behave when they are losing than by how they behave when they are winning? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response argues the comparison rather than praising good behaviour in defeat, which is the trap in this prompt: the claim is that one situation reveals more, and that is what must be defended. Watch for a paper that tests itself against the harder case, since winning well is not effortless either. Structure should be visible enough that a reader can state each paragraph's job after one reading.
accessibility_note: Losing and winning here need not be athletic; an exam, an election for a class role, or a disagreement all provide the material.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The list on the noticeboard had my name on it, and I was certain I had not signed up."
guidance: A strong story chooses quickly what the list is for and then commits, because a candidate still deciding at the halfway mark will not reach an ending. Reward writing that keeps the practical question alive, whether the narrator corrects the mistake or lets it stand. Concrete surroundings, and other people who react, matter more here than an explanation of how the name got there.
accessibility_note: Noticeboards and sign-up lists are described plainly enough in the sentence itself that a student unfamiliar with them can picture the situation.

prompt: When a group is working toward a shared goal, which matters more: that everyone gets heard, or that a decision gets made quickly? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response names the conditions under which its answer holds rather than claiming one is always right, and the best papers say what would change their mind. Particular episodes, with the actual disagreement described, are far more persuasive than general statements about how groups behave. Look for transitions that carry the argument forward instead of merely announcing a new paragraph.
accessibility_note: Any shared task supplies the example, including a class project or a group deciding where to go, so no experience of formal committees is needed.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "For the third morning in a row, someone had left the window open."
guidance: A strong story does one small thing well; the repetition in the opening line is an invitation to a single morning, not to three summarized ones. Look for physical detail that makes the room and the weather real, and for a narrator whose interest in the open window tells us something about them. An ending that leaves the cause unexplained is fine as long as something has been settled.
accessibility_note: The premise needs only a window and a habit, so it can be set in any home, school, or workplace the student can picture.

prompt: Do you agree that it is better to be the person who asks the obvious question than the person who pretends to understand? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response does not treat this as a question with one respectable answer, and the more interesting papers take the cost of asking seriously before deciding. Development beats range here: one classroom or workplace moment told fully will outscore a list of situations. The conclusion should follow from the reasoning rather than repeat the opening sentence in new words.
accessibility_note: The prompt is about what a person does in a room where something was not understood, which is a situation every student has been in regardless of school or country.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The photograph was of our street, but everything in it was in the wrong place."
guidance: A strong story resists explaining the photograph and stays with the person holding it, since the interest is in what they do next. Watch for pacing, because a candidate who catalogues every difference will spend the whole time on the picture. The best responses let the narrator's reaction reveal something about how well they actually know the street.
accessibility_note: Any street the student can imagine will serve, and the sentence assumes no camera, no photographs of one's own, and no particular kind of neighbourhood.

prompt: Some believe a rule should apply the same way to everyone, even when following it exactly produces a result that seems unfair. Others believe a rule should bend when the result would be unfair. Which do you think is right? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response engages with what its own position costs instead of pretending the other side has nothing to say, and the strongest name the loss and argue it is worth accepting. A paper that defines when a bend counts as fairness and when it counts as favouritism is doing the hard part of this prompt. Examples should be specific cases, not claims about what people generally think.
accessibility_note: Deadlines, queues, and classroom procedures all supply examples, so the prompt needs no knowledge of law, government, or any particular country's institutions.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "We had twenty minutes to get there, and the map on the wall was the only one in the building."
guidance: A strong story uses the clock the opening line starts and lets the pressure shape the scene rather than describing it. Look for a we that is actually two or more people with different ideas, since the disagreement is more interesting than the route. Whether they arrive matters less than whether the ending is earned by what happened on the way.
accessibility_note: The sentence supplies the urgency and the obstacle, and no knowledge of any real place, transport system, or building is required.

prompt: Some people believe you should say what you think as soon as you think it. Others believe an opinion is worth more once it has been held quietly for a while. Which do you believe? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response distinguishes waiting from silence, because the prompt is easy to answer as though the alternative were never speaking at all. The best papers use a case where the writer's own timing turned out well or badly, described closely enough that the reader can judge it too. Paragraphs should each do a distinct job rather than circle the same claim.
accessibility_note: Classroom discussion, a conversation with a friend, or a written message all provide the material, and no student is disadvantaged by how talkative their environment is.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The prize was smaller than I had imagined it, and I could not stop looking at it."
guidance: A strong story lets the gap between the imagined prize and the real one carry the meaning without announcing it in the final line. Reward writing that grounds the moment in a place and an audience, since who else is watching changes everything here. Dialogue, if used, should sound like people who were also there rather than like an explanation of the theme.
accessibility_note: The prize is deliberately unspecified, so a student can make it a certificate, a small trophy, or a token, none of which assume a particular kind of competition.

prompt: Do you agree that being trusted with something is a better reward than being praised for something? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response notices that trust arrives as work and says so, because a paper that treats both as pleasant has not found the tension. Look for a writer who has been on both sides and can compare them concretely rather than in the abstract. The best papers acknowledge that praise does something trust does not, and explain why it still matters less.
accessibility_note: Being given a responsibility of any size, at school, at a job, or among friends, is enough to answer, and no formal position or title is assumed.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The bell rang, everyone stood up, and only then did I realize the room was not the one I was supposed to be in."
guidance: A strong story keeps its scope to the minutes after that realization rather than backing up to explain how the mistake happened. Watch for a narrator with a real voice, since embarrassment is a state that writing can either show or merely name. The ending should come from a decision the narrator makes, not from someone else resolving it for them.
accessibility_note: The situation of being in the wrong room needs no familiarity with any particular school system, and the sentence itself supplies the bell and the crowd.

prompt: Some argue that a school should teach a subject because it will be useful later. Others argue that a school should teach a subject because it is interesting now. Which should guide what a school teaches? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response answers as though it had to defend the choice to someone who would live with the consequences, which rules out simply listing the subjects the writer enjoys. The strongest papers admit that usefulness is hard to predict, or that interest is hard to guarantee, and argue anyway. Organization matters here because the two grounds blur together easily.
accessibility_note: Every student has sat in lessons of both kinds, so the prompt draws on ordinary schooling rather than on any particular curriculum or country.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The old clock in the hallway had been stopped for years, and this morning it was right."
guidance: A strong story trusts the reader to feel the coincidence without a paragraph explaining it, and the best ones are more interested in the person noticing than in the clock. Look for concrete detail about the hallway, the hour, and who else passes through. A quiet ending in which nothing supernatural is confirmed can be stronger than a revelation.
accessibility_note: A stopped clock showing the correct time twice a day is a fact the sentence hands the reader, so no specialist knowledge is needed to see why the morning is strange.

prompt: Do you agree that people pay more attention to what someone does once than to what someone does every day? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response separates what people notice from what actually matters, since the claim is about attention and a paper that argues about worth has drifted. Reward a writer who supplies a case of steady work going unremarked and a case of a single act being remembered, and then compares them. Watch for generalizations about society standing in for evidence.
accessibility_note: Examples can come from a classroom, a household chore, or a story the student has read, so nothing about public life or the news is required.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "She handed me the key and said only that I should not use it before Friday."
guidance: A strong story decides whether the instruction is obeyed and builds toward that, rather than spending twenty-five minutes on speculation about the key. Look for restraint: the person who gave it can stay mostly offstage and be more interesting for it. The ending should turn on the narrator's choice about the waiting, not on what is behind the door.
accessibility_note: The sentence gives the whole premise, and a key to something unspecified assumes no property, travel, or particular household.

prompt: Some believe the person who tells you what you did wrong is the better friend. Others believe encouragement does more for a person than correction. Which do you agree with? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response avoids the easy settlement that a friend should do both and commits to one, which is what the prompt asks for. The best papers specify when their answer applies, since the same remark lands differently before an attempt and after one. Look for examples that describe what was actually said and what followed, rather than reporting that a friend was supportive.
accessibility_note: The prompt concerns how friends speak to one another and asks for nothing private about the writer, their family, or any named person.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "There were footprints going up the hill and none coming back down."
guidance: A strong story keeps its scale small, because a candidate who launches a search party will be summarizing by the second page. Reward detail that makes the ground, the light, and the walking real, and a narrator with a reason to be on the hill at all. The best responses accept that the explanation may not arrive and give the reader an ending anyway.
accessibility_note: A hill and a set of footprints need no particular landscape or climate knowledge; snow, mud, or sand all work, and the writer chooses.

prompt: Do you agree that a promise made carelessly is worse than no promise at all? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response defines carelessly early, because the argument depends on whether the writer means thoughtlessly, or generously but without checking. The strongest papers concede that a promise often produces the effort that keeps it, and answer that objection instead of ignoring it. Concrete promises, with what was expected and what arrived, will do more work than statements about honesty in general.
accessibility_note: Everyday promises among friends or classmates supply everything the prompt needs, and no situation involving family obligations has to be disclosed.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The recording was three seconds long, and everyone in the room heard something different on it."
guidance: A strong story uses the disagreement, giving at least two people a version and letting the difference between them matter. Watch for a writer who resolves it too fast; the three seconds are more useful unsettled. The best responses end with the narrator's own hearing changed, whether or not the recording is ever explained.
accessibility_note: The sentence assumes only that a short recording exists and that people are listening together, with no device, platform, or technical knowledge required.

prompt: Some people believe a person's work should be judged by its results. Others believe it should be judged by the effort that went into it. Which is fairer? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response takes on the practical objection that effort cannot be seen from outside, since any answer favouring effort has to say how it would be measured. The strongest papers distinguish the situations, arguing that one standard is fairer for learners and the other for finished work, and then still choose. A reader should be able to state the writer's rule and apply it to a new case.
accessibility_note: Marked schoolwork, a shared task, or a game all supply examples, so the question does not depend on employment or on any particular grading system.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "By the time I noticed the mistake, forty people had already copied it down."
guidance: A strong story stays with the few minutes in which the narrator decides whether to speak, which is where the whole interest of the opening line lies. Look for a specific mistake with specific consequences rather than an unnamed error. An ending in which the narrator says nothing can be as strong as one in which they do, provided the writer has shown what it cost.
accessibility_note: The room can be a classroom, a meeting, or a rehearsal, and the sentence supplies the audience, so nothing about the writer's schooling is assumed.
